questions.q: What is the purpose of a `requirements.txt` file?
options: It stores the actual source code of every dependency
It lists a project's dependencies (and typically their versions) so anyone can recreate the same environment with one command
It's a Python script that runs the project
It's a required file for Python itself to run, even in projects with no dependencies
questions.explain: requirements.txt is a plain list of dependencies that pip can install in one command, making an environment reproducible on any other machine.

options: Deletes all installed packages
Lists every package currently installed in the active environment, at its exact installed version, and writes that list to the file
Installs every package listed inside requirements.txt
Pauses (freezes) the virtual environment so no more packages can be installed
questions.explain: pip freeze prints the installed packages and their exact versions; redirecting that output with > captures the current environment's state into a file.

questions.q: What command installs every package listed in `requirements.txt` into the currently active environment?
options: pip install requirements.txt
pip freeze requirements.txt
pip install -r requirements.txt
python requirements.txt
questions.explain: The -r flag tells pip to read package names (and versions) from the given file and install each one, rather than treating the argument as a single package name.

questions.q: What's the key difference between `requests==2.31.0` and `requests>=2.31.0` in a requirements file?
options: `==` pins that exact version only; `>=` allows that version or any newer one, which can drift over time
They behave identically in every case
`>=` is invalid syntax in requirements.txt
`==` installs from a different package registry than `>=`
questions.explain: == fixes an exact version for maximum reproducibility, while >= permits upgrades to newer releases, which is more flexible but less predictable across installs over time.

questions.q: Why would an application you deploy typically prefer `==` pinning over `>=` ranges in its requirements file?
options: == pinning is required by Python's syntax rules
`>=` ranges are not supported by pip at all
Pinning guarantees every install (your machine, a teammate's, a server) gets identical dependency versions, avoiding version-drift surprises
== pinning makes the application run faster at runtime
questions.explain: For a deployed application, reproducibility matters more than flexibility: == pinning ensures the exact same dependency versions everywhere, whereas a range could silently install a newer (and potentially behavior-changing) version later.
